questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 6 hour history of constant, severe epigastric pain that bores through to his back. He has vomited six times and is sweating. He sits hunched forward on the trolley. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. There is epigastric tenderness without guarding and bowel sounds are reduced.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, eased by leaning forward, with vomiting is acute pancreatitis. Perforation would give a rigid, guarded abdomen.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: epigastric pain that bores through to his back
steps.x: Epigastric pain **radiating to the back**, eased **leaning forward**, vomiting and reduced bowel sounds is the classic pancreatic picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute pancreatitis: confirm with amylase or lipase.

elim: Expect profound shock and a pulsatile mass; his BP is maintained.
Pain would be RUQ with Murphy's sign, not epigastric boring to the back.
Can cause epigastric pain, but not back radiation relieved by sitting forward with reduced bowel sounds.
Gives sudden peritonitis with board-like rigidity; he has no guarding.

steps.x: **D. Acute pancreatitis.** Epigastric pain to the back + leaning forward + vomiting = pancreatitis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem:
A 34 year old woman with familial hyperlipidaemia stopped her medication 6 months ago. She has a 1 day history of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back with vomiting. She drinks no alcohol. Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder with no stones.

Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Triglycerides above 11 mmol/L are a recognised cause of acute pancreatitis once gallstones and alcohol have been excluded.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
With gallstones and alcohol (the two commonest causes) excluded, the very high triglyceride is the cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis.

elim: She drinks no alcohol.
Ultrasound shows no stones.
A recognised cause, but her calcium is normal.
She is not taking it; her lipid result explains the attack.

steps.x: **D. Hypertriglyceridaemia.** No gallstones and no alcohol: look for triglycerides, drugs and recent ERCP.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with ulcerative colitis started a new medication 3 weeks ago for a flare. She now has 12 hours of epigastric pain radiating to her back and vomiting. She drinks no alcohol. Ultrasound shows no gallstones. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Her serum amylase is 1,450 U/L (<100).
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused this?
questions.e: Aminosalicylates (mesalazine, sulfasalazine) are recognised drug causes of acute pancreatitis; the other drugs are not.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
A young non-drinker with no stones and a new UC drug: think of the aminosalicylates.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mesalazine (an aminosalicylate, like sulfasalazine).

elim: Not associated with pancreatitis.
Antimotility agent; not a recognised cause.
Not a recognised cause of pancreatitis.
Hepatotoxic in overdose but does not cause pancreatitis.

steps.x: **C. Mesalazine.** Drug causes to know: co-trimoxazole, sulfasalazine, mesalazine, sodium valproate.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with HIV is taking a sulfonamide antibiotic as prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia. He has a 2 day history of epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. He does not drink alcohol and ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. His lipase is 1,980 U/L (<160).
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused this?
questions.e: Co-trimoxazole is a sulfonamide antibiotic used for PCP prophylaxis and is a recognised drug cause of acute pancreatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
PCP prophylaxis with a sulfonamide is co-trimoxazole, a known cause of pancreatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Co-trimoxazole.

elim: Not a sulfonamide and not a recognised cause.
Macrolide; not used for PCP prophylaxis and not a classic cause.
Tetracycline; not a sulfonamide.
Used for UTIs and not a sulfonamide.

steps.x: **C. Co-trimoxazole.** Sulfonamide antibiotic (co-trimoxazole) = drug cause of acute pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with a BMI of 34 has had several episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals over the past year. She now has 10 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back. She drinks 2 units of alcohol a week. Her ALT is 310 U/L (<40) and amylase 2,100 U/L (<100). Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her pancreatitis?
questions.e: Previous biliary colic, a raised ALT and a dilated CBD indicate gallstone pancreatitis; she does not drink to excess.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
steps.x: Previous biliary colic, a high ALT and a dilated CBD point to a stone passing through the ampulla.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallstone pancreatitis.

elim: 2 units a week is not excess.
No lipid history; the biliary story explains it.
Would give painless jaundice and weight loss, not prior biliary colic.
A rare cause; nothing here suggests it.

steps.x: **B. Gallstones.** Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest causes; a raised ALT favours gallstones.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has severe epigastric pain radiating to his back that started this morning. Over the past week he had a colonoscopy, an outpatient OGD and, 18 hours ago, a procedure to remove a common bile duct stone. He drinks no alcohol. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. His amylase is 1,760 U/L (<100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pancreatitis?
questions.e: Acute pancreatitis is the most common complication of ERCP, and the onset hours after stone removal fits. OGD and colonoscopy do not cannulate the ampulla.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: remove a common bile duct stone
steps.x: CBD stones are removed at ERCP, and pancreatitis is its most common complication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-ERCP pancreatitis.

elim: Does not instrument the pancreatic duct.
The stone has already been removed; the timing points to the procedure.
No lipid history given.
Does not cannulate the ampulla.

steps.x: **E. Recent ERCP.** Pancreatitis hours after ERCP = post-ERCP pancreatitis, the commonest ERCP complication.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 8 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and repeated vomiting after a large meal. She finds lying flat makes the pain worse. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Her lipase is 3,100 U/L (<160).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Board-like rigidity with loss of liver dullness
Epigastric tenderness with reduced bowel sounds
Tender mass in the left iliac fossa
questions.e: Acute pancreatitis gives epigastric tenderness and reduced bowel sounds from an ileus. Rigidity with loss of liver dullness is perforation.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: lying flat makes the pain worse
steps.x: Confirmed pancreatitis; the retroperitoneal inflammation gives epigastric tenderness and an ileus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Epigastric tenderness and reduced bowel sounds.

elim: Signs of a perforated viscus.
A sign of appendicitis.
Suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Suggests a diverticular abscess.

steps.x: **B. Epigastric tenderness with reduced bowel sounds.** Pancreatitis exam: epigastric tenderness, reduced bowel sounds; severe cases add tachycardia, hypotension, distension.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is on day 4 of admission with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis. He has become mildly breathless. There is reduced air entry and stony dullness at the left base. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 4
visual.caption: Blunted left costophrenic angle with a meniscus: left pleural effusion.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Capillary leak in pancreatitis moves fluid into third spaces, and a left pleural effusion is typical. ARDS would be bilateral.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: stony dullness at the left base
steps.x: Fluid leaking into third spaces in pancreatitis typically collects as a **left pleural effusion**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pleural effusion from third-space losses.

elim: Gives bilateral diffuse shadowing and severe hypoxia, not a unilateral basal effusion.
Would give consolidation with crackles and fever, not stony dullness.
Hyper-resonant, not stony dull.
The X-ray is often normal; stony dullness indicates fluid.

steps.x: **C. Pleural effusion.** Stony dull base in pancreatitis = third-space fluid as a pleural effusion.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman is on day 2 of admission with severe gallstone pancreatitis. She becomes increasingly breathless despite oxygen. She has bilateral crackles. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% on 40% oxygen. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: Capillary leak causes ARDS, seen as bilateral ground-glass opacities with a normal heart. The other findings do not explain bilateral crackles and refractory hypoxia.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Severe hypoxia with bilateral crackles and a normal heart in severe pancreatitis is ARDS from pulmonary capillary leak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ARDS: bilateral ground-glass opacities (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema).

elim: Indicates perforation, not a respiratory cause of hypoxia.
Gives unilateral signs, not bilateral crackles and profound hypoxia.
Suggests TB or abscess; not acute.
Gives unilateral reduced air entry and hyper-resonance.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities.** Severe pancreatitis + refractory hypoxia + normal heart = ARDS: bilateral ground-glass change.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is on day 6 of admission with severe alcohol-related pancreatitis. After initial improvement he is now febrile and more unwell. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a large area of pancreatic parenchyma that does not enhance.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Necrosis develops in the first week and appears as non-enhancing parenchyma on CT; new sepsis suggests infection. A pseudocyst forms from about 4 weeks.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Non-enhancing tissue = non-viable pancreas (necrosis), developing in the first week. New fever suggests infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infected pancreatic necrosis.

elim: Needs jaundice and a dilated duct; the CT finding is in the pancreas.
Presents with painless jaundice and weight loss over weeks.
Forms from about 4 weeks as a walled-off fluid collection.
A vascular complication; it does not cause non-enhancing parenchyma.

steps.x: **B. Infected pancreatic necrosis.** Non-enhancing pancreas in week 1 = necrosis; fever and deterioration = infected necrosis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man was treated for acute pancreatitis 5 weeks ago. He now has dull epigastric pain, bloating, indigestion and early satiety. He has mild scleral icterus. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Abdominal examination shows a vague epigastric fullness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic ulcer
questions.e: A pseudocyst develops about 4 weeks after pancreatitis with dull pain, bloating, indigestion and mild jaundice. Necrosis occurs in the first week.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
About 4 weeks after pancreatitis with dull pain, bloating, mild jaundice and a mass: a walled-off collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pancreatic pseudocyst.

elim: Develops over years with steatorrhoea and diabetes, not a mass 5 weeks after one episode.
No ulcer history; the timing after pancreatitis is the clue.
Possible with jaundice and a mass, but the 4–6 week timing after pancreatitis points to a pseudocyst.
Develops within the first week, not at 5 weeks.

steps.x: **E. Pancreatic pseudocyst.** Around 4 weeks after pancreatitis with persistent symptoms and a mass = pseudocyst.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman had gallstone pancreatitis 6 weeks ago. Her amylase has stayed raised at 540 U/L (<100). She has dull epigastric pain and bloating. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Her WCC is 12.4 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0). A CT abdomen is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT?
o: Dilated common bile and pancreatic ducts
Well-defined fluid-filled collection next to the pancreas
questions.e: A pseudocyst shows on CT as a dense fluid-filled mass and causes a persistently raised amylase about 4 weeks after an attack. Non-enhancing parenchyma is necrosis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
A persistently raised amylase weeks after pancreatitis with pain and bloating suggests a pseudocyst.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A fluid-filled collection: pseudocyst.

elim: A feature of chronic pancreatitis.
The double duct sign of a pancreatic head tumour.
Pneumobilia, as in gallstone ileus or after sphincterotomy.
Necrosis, which develops in the first week.

steps.x: **E. Well-defined fluid-filled collection next to the pancreas.** Persistently raised amylase from about 4 weeks + CT fluid-filled mass = pseudocyst.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man is on day 3 of admission with severe pancreatitis. While his blood pressure is being measured his hand goes into spasm, with flexion at the wrist. He reports tingling around his mouth. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. CT on admission showed extensive peripancreatic fat necrosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely electrolyte abnormality?
questions.e: Fat necrosis binds circulating calcium (saponification), causing hypocalcaemia with tetany. Calcium <2 mmol/L is a Glasgow severity marker.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Carpopedal spasm with a BP cuff (Trousseau's sign) and perioral tingling mean tetany: low calcium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypocalcaemia.

elim: A cause of pancreatitis, but it does not cause tetany.
Causes ECG changes and weakness, not carpopedal spasm.
Causes confusion and thirst, not tetany.
Causes weakness and arrhythmias, not perioral tingling.

steps.x: **D. Hypocalcaemia.** Fat necrosis binds calcium (saponification); calcium <2 mmol/L scores on the Glasgow criteria.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man is brought in with his third episode in 2 years of severe epigastric pain going through to his back. He drinks about 70 units of alcohol a week, has lost his appetite and is sweating. His abdomen is distended. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. His amylase is 1,320 U/L (<100). The site of pain is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric pain boring through to the back.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent episodes, heavy drinking, anorexia and an amylase over 3 times normal indicate acute alcoholic pancreatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: lost his appetite and is sweating
steps.x: Repeated similar episodes, heavy alcohol use, anorexia, sweating and an amylase over 3x normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute alcoholic pancreatitis.

elim: Gives jaundice and tender hepatomegaly, not a very high amylase.
Epigastric pain, but amylase would not be 13 times normal.
Presents with haematemesis after retching.
Gives peritonism; a modest amylase rise can occur, but not this pattern of recurrent attacks.

steps.x: **A. Acute alcoholic pancreatitis.** Recurrent attacks in a heavy drinker with amylase >3x normal = acute alcoholic pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has 5 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back with vomiting. She is lying still and leaning forward. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There is epigastric tenderness. An ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: The initial diagnostic test is serum amylase (or lipase) at 3 times the upper limit of normal. Ultrasound is then used to look for gallstones.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Clinical picture of pancreatitis: confirm with a raised pancreatic enzyme.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Serum amylase (or lipase).

elim: Done next to look for gallstones as the cause, not to confirm the diagnosis.
Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected complications.
Non-specific; does not confirm pancreatitis.
The ECG is normal and the picture is pancreatic.

steps.x: **C. Serum amylase.** Clinical picture + amylase or lipase >3x upper limit of normal confirms pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has 4 days of epigastric pain radiating to his back with vomiting. He only came in today. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. His amylase is 160 U/L (<100). His GP suspects acute pancreatitis.
questions.q: Which result would best confirm acute pancreatitis?
o: Amylase more than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal
Lipase more than 3 times the upper limit of normal
questions.e: Lipase stays elevated longer than amylase and is more specific, so a lipase over 3 times the upper limit of normal confirms a late presentation.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Amylase falls quickly; after 4 days it may be near normal. Lipase stays raised for longer and is more specific.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lipase above 3x the upper limit of normal.

elim: One of the Glasgow severity criteria; it does not diagnose pancreatitis.
Too low a threshold; 3x is needed.
A severity marker, not diagnostic.
Indicates severity or inflammation, not the diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Lipase more than 3 times the upper limit of normal.** Late presentation: lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man drinks 40 units of alcohol a week. He has acute pancreatitis confirmed with a lipase of 2,640 U/L (<160). His pain is controlled and he is receiving IV fluids. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. His bilirubin and ALT are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Early ultrasound is used in all patients to look for gallstones, which would need cholecystectomy, even when alcohol seems the obvious cause.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Even in a drinker, gallstones must be excluded early because they change management (cholecystectomy).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Abdominal ultrasound.

elim: Not needed when the diagnosis is clear and there are no complications.
Therapeutic; only for obstruction or cholangitis.
Looks for perforation; the diagnosis is already confirmed.
Second-line biliary imaging if ultrasound is inconclusive.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Every case of pancreatitis gets an early ultrasound to look for gallstones.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has 2 days of epigastric and back pain with vomiting. He has a history of an abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. His amylase is 210 U/L (<100) and lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0). Bedside ultrasound is limited by bowel gas.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When the diagnosis is uncertain (amylase below 3x and an aneurysm to exclude), CT abdomen is the next test.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Amylase only twice normal and other serious diagnoses possible: the diagnosis is uncertain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT abdomen.

elim: Does not show the pancreas or the aorta well.
Images the stomach lumen; not useful for an uncertain acute abdomen.
Examines the colon; not relevant to epigastric and back pain.
Images the ducts; slow and not the test for an uncertain acute abdomen.

steps.x: **D. CT abdomen.** Diagnosis uncertain or complications suspected: CT abdomen.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman is admitted with acute gallstone pancreatitis. Her lipase is 2,900 U/L (<160). Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. The team wants to calculate the Modified Glasgow (Imrie) score to judge severity.
questions.q: When should the score be calculated?
questions.e: The Modified Glasgow (Imrie) criteria are calculated at 48 hours. Emergency features such as shock still need escalation before then.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
The Modified Glasgow (Imrie) criteria are assessed over the first 48 hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: At 48 hours.

elim: Too early; the score is validated at 48 hours.
Far too early; values are still evolving.
Too late to guide early escalation.
The score is clinical and biochemical; it does not need CT.

steps.x: **B. At 48 hours after admission.** Glasgow-Imrie: calculated at 48 hours; ≥3 = severe.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has acute pancreatitis. At 48 hours, his WCC is 13.2 × 10⁹/L, adjusted calcium 2.18 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L, glucose 9.1 mmol/L and LDH 420 U/L. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. The registrar says one result is missing to complete the Glasgow-Imrie score.
questions.q: Which investigation is needed to complete the score?
questions.e: PaO2 <8 kPa is the 'P' of PANCREAS and needs an ABG. Amylase and lipase diagnose pancreatitis but are not part of the score.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
PANCREAS: PaO2, Age, Neutrophils, Calcium, Urea, Enzymes (LDH/AST), Albumin, Sugar. Only PaO2 is missing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial blood gas (PaO2 <8 kPa scores).

elim: Amylase confirms the diagnosis but is not in the Glasgow score.
Not one of the PANCREAS criteria.
A severity marker in some systems but not in Glasgow-Imrie.
Diagnostic, not part of the score.

steps.x: **A. Arterial blood gas for PaO2.** Remember PANCREAS; amylase and lipase are NOT in the severity score.

questions.stem:
A 62 year old woman has acute pancreatitis from gallstones. Results at 48 hours are shown. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.

Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the severity of her pancreatitis?
questions.e: Age over 55 and urea over 16 give a Glasgow-Imrie score of 2, which is moderate. A score of 3 or more would be severe.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Age >55 (1) and urea >16 (1). WCC 13, calcium 2.2, albumin 35, glucose 8, LDH 400 and PaO2 10.5 do not score.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Score 2: moderate.

elim: She meets at least age and urea.
Age >55 alone would be 1, but urea >16 adds another.
Only two criteria are met.
Calcium, WCC, albumin, glucose, LDH and PaO2 are within the thresholds.

steps.x: **C. Moderate, score 2.** Glasgow-Imrie 0–1 mild, 2 moderate, ≥3 severe.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man is admitted with acute alcohol-related pancreatitis. The admitting team wants a severity score that can be calculated within 24 hours using BUN, impaired mental status, SIRS, age and pleural effusion. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which severity score are they using?
questions.e: BISAP (BUN, Impaired mental status, SIRS, Age, Pleural effusion) is a pancreatitis severity score, alongside Glasgow-Imrie and Ranson's criteria.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: BUN, impaired mental status, SIRS, age and pleural effusion
steps.x: BISAP = BUN, Impaired mental status, SIRS, Age, Pleural effusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BISAP.

elim: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
Pneumonia severity.
Upper GI bleeding risk.
Probability of DVT or PE.

steps.x: **A. BISAP score.** Pancreatitis severity: Glasgow-Imrie (main, at 48 h), Ranson's and BISAP.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has 6 hours of epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. His lipase is 3,800 U/L (<160). His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Ultrasound has been requested but is not yet done.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Initial management is crystalloid resuscitation (Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline 500 mL stat with review), started before imaging, with opioid analgesia and oxygen if hypoxic.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Tachycardic and borderline hypotensive: fluid resuscitation starts before imaging.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV crystalloid (Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline) 500 mL stat, then review.

elim: Imaging must not delay resuscitation; CT is not needed when the diagnosis is clear.
Antibiotics are not routine in pancreatitis.
Crystalloid, not albumin, is the first-line fluid.
Only for biliary obstruction or cholangitis.

steps.x: **D. Rapid IV crystalloid 500 mL stat.** Pancreatitis: crystalloid resuscitation first, even before imaging, plus opioid analgesia and oxygen if hypoxic.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has acute gallstone pancreatitis. She has received 1 L of IV Hartmann's solution. She is still in severe pain, scoring 9 out of 10. Her pulse rate is 102 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Opioid analgesia is used for pancreatic pain, and oxygen is added because her saturation is 91%.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
After fluids, give opioid analgesia, and oxygen because she is hypoxic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV opioid plus oxygen.

elim: An antispasmodic; it does not control severe pancreatic pain.
She is hypoxic, so she also needs oxygen.
Too weak, and ignores her hypoxia.
Inadequate for 9/10 pancreatic pain.

steps.x: **C. IV morphine and supplemental oxygen.** Pancreatitis supportive care: fluids, opioid analgesia, oxygen if hypoxic.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man was admitted 20 hours ago with mild alcohol-related pancreatitis (Glasgow score 0 expected). His pain is now controlled on oral analgesia and he says he is hungry. He is not vomiting. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. His amylase is still 640 U/L (<100).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate nutritional management?
o: Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage
Keep nil by mouth until amylase is normal
Offer an oral diet as tolerated
questions.e: Oral feeding is started early, within 24 hours, as tolerated. Waiting for the amylase to normalise is not needed.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Mild disease, hungry and not vomiting: feed by mouth early.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral feeding as tolerated, within 24 hours.

elim: Only for persistent vomiting or ileus.
Outdated; amylase level does not guide feeding.
Tube feeding is for moderately severe or severe disease.
Reserved for when enteral feeding is impossible.

steps.x: **C. Offer an oral diet as tolerated.** Start oral feeding early (within 24 hours) as tolerated; do not wait for amylase to fall.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman is on day 3 in HDU with severe gallstone pancreatitis (Glasgow score 4). She has persistent nausea and cannot manage oral intake. Her gut is functioning, with bowel sounds present. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate nutritional support?
o: Continue nil by mouth with IV dextrose
questions.e: Enteral nutrition is offered in moderately severe or severe pancreatitis when oral intake is not possible; parenteral feeding is reserved for when enteral fails.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Severe disease, unable to eat, functioning gut: tube feeding into the gut.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Enteral (nasogastric or nasojejunal) nutrition.

elim: Leaves her malnourished; nutrition is needed in severe disease.
She cannot manage oral intake.
Used only if enteral feeding fails or is not tolerated.
Amylase does not guide feeding.

steps.x: **B. Enteral tube feeding.** Moderately severe or severe pancreatitis: offer enteral nutrition; parenteral only if enteral fails.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man is on day 2 of admission with mild alcohol-related pancreatitis. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. His CRP is 96 mg/L (<5) and WCC 12.1 × 10⁹/L (4.0–11.0). Chest X-ray and urine dip are normal. A junior doctor asks whether to start antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue fluids and analgesia without antibiotics
questions.e: Antibiotics are not routine in pancreatitis; fever and raised CRP reflect inflammation. They are only for infected necrosis, cholangitis or another confirmed infection.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: Chest X-ray and urine dip are normal
steps.x: Low-grade fever and raised CRP are part of the inflammatory response, not proof of infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Supportive care, no antibiotics.

elim: No infection is confirmed; antibiotics are not routine.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.
No indication for antibiotics.
No obstruction or cholangitis; this is alcohol-related.

steps.x: **A. Continue fluids and analgesia without antibiotics.** Antibiotics only for infected necrosis, cholangitis or another confirmed infection.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman is on day 12 of severe pancreatitis. She has swinging fevers and has deteriorated. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. CT shows a necrotic pancreatic collection containing gas bubbles. Blood cultures are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: IV antibiotics and drainage of the necrosis
questions.e: Gas in a necrotic collection with sepsis means infected necrosis, which needs IV antibiotics and drainage or debridement.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Gas in necrosis with sepsis = infected necrosis: an indication for antibiotics plus drainage or debridement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV antibiotics with drainage or debridement.

elim: Infected necrosis is life-threatening and needs treatment.
Treats the cause later; not the emergency.
Inadequate for septic infected necrosis.
Not the standard approach; step-up drainage or debridement is used.

steps.x: **C. IV antibiotics and drainage of the necrosis.** Infected necrosis is the main indication for antibiotics; it also needs drainage or debridement.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is admitted with gallstone pancreatitis. Over 24 hours his bilirubin rises from 40 to 96 µmol/L (<21). He has no fever. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct of 11 mm with a stone at its lower end.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: ERCP clears an obstructing CBD stone in gallstone pancreatitis. Cholecystectomy follows after recovery to stop it happening again.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: dilated common bile duct of 11 mm with a stone
steps.x: An obstructing CBD stone with rising bilirubin needs the duct cleared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ERCP to remove the stone.

elim: The cause is already shown on ultrasound.
Does not clear the CBD stone and is not done in the acute phase.
There is no cholangitis, and the obstruction needs relieving.
Leaves an obstructed duct with rising bilirubin.

steps.x: **C. ERCP.** ERCP for biliary obstruction or cholangitis in gallstone pancreatitis; cholecystectomy after recovery.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman is recovering from mild gallstone pancreatitis. Her pain has settled and she is eating normally. Her LFTs are normal. Ultrasound showed multiple small gallstones and a normal calibre common bile duct. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. She asks how to stop it happening again.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Cholecystectomy after recovery removes the source of stones. ERCP is only for duct obstruction or cholangitis.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Gallstone pancreatitis recurs unless the gallbladder is removed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cholecystectomy after recovery.

elim: Does not remove the stones; recurrence risk remains.
Slow and unreliable; not standard.
For exocrine insufficiency, not gallstones.
Not needed when the duct is clear and LFTs are normal.

steps.x: **A. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy once recovered.** Gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy after recovery (usually the same admission).

questions.stem: A 66 year old man was admitted 10 hours ago with acute pancreatitis. Despite 2 L of IV crystalloid he is confused. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. His urine output is 10 mL/hour. The Glasgow score cannot yet be calculated.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Calculate the Glasgow score at 48 hours before deciding
Transfer to the ward with 4-hourly observations
questions.e: Shock, hypoxia and organ failure are emergency features that need escalation to HDU/ICU without waiting for the 48-hour Glasgow score.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Shock, hypoxia and oliguria are emergency features of organ failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Escalate to HDU/ICU now.

elim: Shock and hypoxia need escalation now.
Not a treatment for pancreatitis.
Unsafe; he has organ failure.
Does not treat organ failure and is not done acutely.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to critical care.** Shock, hypoxia, organ failure or sepsis = escalate to critical care, the same as Glasgow ≥3.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had alcohol-related pancreatitis 5 weeks ago. A CT shows a 5 cm well-defined fluid collection next to the pancreas. He has only mild bloating and is eating normally. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. His bilirubin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Pseudocysts are managed conservatively at first because they often resolve. Drainage is reserved for symptomatic, communicating cysts.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: only mild bloating and is eating normally
steps.x: A pseudocyst with minimal symptoms often resolves on its own.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Conservative management with repeat imaging.

elim: Far too radical for a pseudocyst.
Reserved for symptomatic, communicating cysts.
Not first line; it often recurs.
For infected necrosis or symptomatic cysts, not mild symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Conservative management with repeat imaging.** Pseudocyst: conservative first; drain only if symptomatic and communicating.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had gallstone pancreatitis 10 weeks ago. She now has persistent epigastric pain, early satiety and vomiting after meals. CT shows an 11 cm pseudocyst compressing the stomach, and imaging shows it communicates with the pancreatic duct. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Endoscopic drainage (or surgery) is reserved for symptomatic, communicating pseudocysts like this one. Small asymptomatic cysts are observed.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: persistent epigastric pain, early satiety and vomiting
steps.x: A large, symptomatic, communicating pseudocyst will not settle on its own.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endoscopic drainage.

elim: She is symptomatic with gastric compression.
No infection is suggested.
Does not treat a compressive cyst.
A cancer operation, not for a pseudocyst.

steps.x: **B. Endoscopic drainage.** Symptomatic, communicating pseudocyst = endoscopic drainage or surgery.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has acute gallstone pancreatitis. A student asks why the enzyme that triggers the injury does not normally digest the pancreas. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Her lipase is 2,800 U/L (<160).
questions.q: Where is trypsinogen normally converted to trypsin?
questions.e: Trypsinogen is normally activated only in the duodenum. Premature activation in the pancreas activates other proenzymes, causing autodigestion and systemic inflammation.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: why the enzyme that triggers the injury does not normally digest the pancreas
steps.x: Trypsinogen is normally activated only in the duodenum (by enteropeptidase). In pancreatitis it activates early inside the pancreas, then activates other enzymes and causes autodigestion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Duodenum.

elim: Premature activation here is what causes pancreatitis.
Trypsinogen should stay inactive in the ducts.
Enzymes are not activated in the blood.
Pepsin is activated in the stomach, not trypsin.

steps.x: **B. Duodenum.** Pancreatitis = premature intra-pancreatic activation of trypsinogen, normally activated only in the duodenum.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has acute pancreatitis. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct. She drinks no alcohol. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Her ALT is 260 U/L (<40) and amylase 2,450 U/L (<100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pancreatitis?
o: Protein plugs in the pancreatic ducts
Stone obstructing the ampulla of Vater
questions.e: Gallstones obstruct the ampulla of Vater, causing reflux of secretions and raised intraductal pressure. Acinar toxicity and protein plugs are the mechanisms of alcohol.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: gallstones and a dilated common bile duct
steps.x: A stone impacted at the ampulla blocks drainage, causing reflux of bile/pancreatic juice and raised duct pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallstone obstructing the ampulla of Vater.

elim: Autoimmune pancreatitis is rare and IgG4-related.
The mechanism of alcohol, which she does not drink.
Also an alcohol mechanism.
Mumps can cause pancreatitis, but stones are shown here.

steps.x: **D. Stone obstructing the ampulla of Vater.** Gallstones obstruct the ampulla; alcohol is toxic to acinar cells and forms protein plugs.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man who drinks 90 units of alcohol a week has his fourth admission with acute pancreatitis. Ultrasound shows no gallstones and a normal common bile duct. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. His lipase is 1,900 U/L (<160).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pancreatitis?
o: Acinar cell toxicity and protein plugs in the ducts
questions.e: Alcohol injures acinar cells directly and promotes protein plugs in the pancreatic ducts. Ampullary obstruction is the gallstone mechanism.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Alcohol is directly toxic to acinar cells and makes protein plugs that block small ducts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Direct acinar toxicity with ductal protein plugs.

No lipid result is given; alcohol is the obvious cause.

Not the mechanism of alcohol.

steps.x: **A. Acinar cell toxicity and protein plugs in the ducts.** Alcohol: direct acinar injury + protein plugs. Gallstones: ampullary obstruction.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has severe pancreatitis. Despite 4 L of IV fluid in 24 hours she remains hypotensive with a low urine output. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and she has bilateral basal effusions. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. Her haematocrit has risen from 0.42 to 0.50.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypovolaemia?
o: Capillary leak from the systemic inflammatory response
questions.e: The systemic inflammatory response causes capillary leak, moving fluid into third spaces (ascites, effusions) with haemoconcentration and hypovolaemia.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Ascites, effusions and a rising haematocrit despite fluid: plasma is leaking into third spaces.

steps.x: Capillary leak syndrome.

steps.x: **A. Capillary leak from the systemic inflammatory response.** Systemic inflammation → capillary leak → third-space losses and hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a fluid collection next to the pancreas 6 weeks after acute pancreatitis. It is drained endoscopically. Histology of the wall is reported. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. His amylase had remained raised for weeks.

o: Cuboidal epithelium lining a true cyst

steps.x: Fibrous/granulation tissue, no epithelium.

A true cyst has an epithelial lining; a pseudocyst does not.

Not found around the pancreas.

steps.x: **E. Walled-off fibrous tissue without an epithelial lining.** Pseudocyst = 'pseudo' because there is no true epithelial lining.
